entries.title: About the Course
entries.content:
Alveary Modern Language Lessons are designed to mirror the way children acquire their first language, using methods like gestures, picture recognition, songs, repeated phrases, and storytelling to create meaningful connections and context. These foundational approaches are seamlessly adapted to teach school-age children a second language.

The lessons are designed to be open-and-go with optional video/audio file support. They do not require any background in the target language for the parent/teacher or students. They only take about 15-20 min a day and can be easily adjusted to meet a variety of grade ranges from 1st to 6th grades.

entries.title: Placement & Combining Tips
entries.content:
Three lessons each week are shared between Grades 1-6, but students in Grades 4-6 add two additional extension day lessons. This course is on a six-year rotation of lessons, so it is suitable for students who took Lower Spanish last year or students just starting their studies.

Students in grades 4+ who feel anxious about speaking a new language may benefit from taking a year without the added extension days. This approach allows them to build confidence and comfort before focusing on speaking and writing.

blocks.text:
Students will complete a picture study lesson each week. Students will spend two weeks with the same vocabulary and narration sentences. Each lesson has an accompanying video to follow along with the lesson. In these lessons, students will be focused on beginning the skill of narration in another language within the context of discussing a picture from the assigned picture study book. They will use vocabulary and narration series sentences to help them describe what they see. Narration in another language generally follows this progression: 

- Recall - When given the Spanish word, students should be able to identify the given word or phrase by pointing to a picture or making a gesture that demonstrates the word or phrase. 

- Recite - When given a prompt students will learn to respond in Spanish. At this stage, students can be asked to say the narration series as they point to the corresponding image. Likewise they will practice saying the Spanish word for a given image or gesture.

- Compose - As understanding grows, students may begin to notice objects in a picture or in the world around them and be able to describe them using Spanish. Beginning Spanish will be broken, often with improper grammar. That is ok. Much in the same way that children learn how to use proper tense and grammatical structure in speaking their first language, they will develop that here too, but at this stage it should be a byproduct of their learning, rather than the primary focus.

NOTE: While using these lessons and tools, keep the end goal in mind. Students should be working toward using the language to describe pictures in books and the world around them.

In grades 4-6, students are given the option of an additional extension day for picture study lessons. On these extension days, students will review the picture study lessons from the previous day. Students will also receive a gentle introduction to new grammar concepts every other week. Each lesson has an accompanying video to follow along.

Below is what you can expect for the general flow of a lesson:
- Read/watch any preparatory material and look over any student notebook pages or resources that will be used in the lesson. 
- Review the order of the lesson, and pull up any links that will be used in the lesson. 
- Practice the Phrase of the Week. 
- Ask students what they recall from the previous lesson.
- Play the video/audio links provided using the QR code or links page.
- Introduce and practice new vocabulary using TPR (Total Physical Response - using gestures and pointing) and picture recognition.
- Introduce and practice narration sentences, pointing to corresponding images.
For picture study lessons, students can find a Vocabulary Glossary in the reference section of their Student Notebook to follow along as new words are being introduced and for review.

Students will complete one literature lesson per week. In these lessons, students will focus on building listening comprehension. When learning a new language, it can be hard to hear it and understand it at the same time. Students are encouraged to infer the meaning of a phrase or sentence without needing to memorize every word. As vocabulary is introduced, the goal is to build comprehension in context. The literature lessons have more difficult words and sentence structures, but students will begin to recognize the vocabulary words and how they are used through repetition.

In grades 4-6, students are given the option of an additional extension day for literature lessons. These extension days give additional time for students to practice listening to and comprehending the story, repeating what they recall aloud while using TPR, writing the story lines through copywork to become more familiar with the target language in written form, as well as drawing their own storyboards to accompany the story lines.

Below is what you can expect for the general flow of a lesson:
- Read/watch any preparatory material and look over any student notebook pages to familiarize yourself.
- Choose a few sentences or vocabulary words to review at the beginning of each lesson.
- Press play on the video/audio link provided in the QR link page.
- Introduce new vocabulary.
- Practice vocabulary using TPR/point and tell methods.
- Read the story.
- Practice storyline recognition.
- Work on storyboards or copywork.

On the literature pages of the student notebook, you will find storyboard boxes for students to draw their narrations as well as copywork lines for students to write the story lines on extension days. Copywork extension days are only scheduled for Grades 4-6.

Students will complete one Songs, Rhymes, & Conversations lesson per week. In these lessons, students are exposed to cultural songs and rhymes and also given the opportunity to practice singing or saying the language out loud in a fun and engaging way. Students may sometimes feel self-conscious or silly when trying to speak a new language. Singing songs or chanting rhymes can help students overcome these insecurities. Each lesson will include an audio or video file to follow as students learn the song or rhyme. In these lessons, students will also be introduced to simple conversational phrases they can use in the target language.

Below is what you can expect for the general flow of a lesson:
- Read/watch any preparatory material and look over any related student notebook pages.
- Choose a few lines from the song or rhyme being studied, or a conversation phrase or two to review at the beginning of each lesson.
- Open to the current song/rhyme.
- Play the video/audio link provided in the QR link page.
- Practice reciting/singing the passage.
- Introduce the new conversation phrases, following along with any provided audio/video materials and pausing as needed.
- Practice conversation sentences with students or have them practice amongst themselves (or with puppets, props or stuffed animals).
All of the songs, rhymes and conversation sentences or phrases have been provided in the Student Notebook for student and teacher reference.

lessons.cctBlock:
➜ Cultural Topic - La Feria
Most Spanish speaking countries celebrate regional “ferias” or fairs.  Historically they were a method of exchange and market for agricultural or livestock seasons. They usually include food, music, entertainment, religious and artisanal aspects.  They are bright, colorful and typically run for several days

∞ Video Link: [Feria de Sevilla](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aeHaioZ0vbc), Spain: 8 minutes
∞ Video Link: [Feria de Tonatico](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ARJB0f5K1_0), Mexico: 10 minutes 
Tip: You may need to adjust your settings to display English subtitles.

lessons.cctBlock:
➜ CULTURAL TOPIC - Naranjas
In Spanish culture, small portions of the backyard/land are designated for vegetable and fruit patches; these are known as huertos. They are culturally symbolic and practical in homes.  Such things as providing year-round food or shade in mostly desert-like areas, as found in places like Spain or Mexico. They are a source for gathering and tradition.

∞ Video Link: [Cuidados de Naranja](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BaNRNPUziog) (with a grandmother from Spain). The video is in Spanish but enjoy watching her explain her backyard orange tree. Maybe you will pick up some words.
∞ Video Link: A short video on a [boy picking up an orange](https://youtube.com/shorts/uNtB91ily0Y?si=ZJ7kMt1j6hUWsevU) from his grandfather’s backyard

lessons.cctBlock:
➜ CULTURAL TOPIC - Feliz Cumpleaños
Celebrations of birthdays in Spanish culture still maintain many traditions dating decades and with variations based on the country. Celebrations are typically multi-generational, bringing together large extended families

∞ Video Link: The following [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1KoVOiIwk7A) does a wonderful job of explaining many of the Mexican birthday traditions as experienced by an American girl living in Mexico.
∞ Video Link: This [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zDfLQz-zmzA&t=21s) is also has a good explanation of birthday traditions but the speaker explains in Spanish and the words are subtitled in English

➜ CULTURAL TOPIC - Canicas y Trompos
Across Latin America and Spain, they represent a communal, low-cost heritage where kids gather to share stories and trade marbles and play spinning tops.

∞ Video Link: This [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jDF4O_yEQFY) shows a tutorial for a trick with a spinning top “trompos".  Make sure you have the auto translate on for captions.
∞ Video Link: Short [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5V-uOT820vA) of children in Oaxaca playing marbles “canicas”

lessons.cctBlock:
➜ CULTURAL TOPIC - Nopales for Cooking
In Mexican culture, "picando nopales" (dicing cactus pads) represents far more than a culinary step. The prickly pear cactus (nopal) is a profound symbol of resilience and indigenous heritage. It thrives in harsh, arid landscapes and has sustained Mesoamerican communities for thousands of years.

∞ Video Link: This is a [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WJ359L5W988) of a grandma showing how she prepares the nopales she harvests from her home. Remember to have your settings on Spanish to English translation of captions.

lessons.grammarInstructions:
In Spanish, nouns are either “masculine (el/the)” or “feminine (la/the).” 
Masculine nouns typically end in “o,” while feminine nouns typically end in “a.” (There are exceptions.)
lessons.practiceInstructions: Make two columns, label one masculine the other feminine. Using this week's vocabulary words, sort the nouns into the correct column.

lessons.grammarInstructions:
➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Adjectives & Agreement
In Spanish, adjectives must match the noun they describe in both gender (masculine/feminine) and number (singular/plural). Generally, adjectives ending in -o change to -a for feminine, and both add -s or -es to become plural. Adjectives ending in -e or a consonant usually remain the same for gender but change for number.

➜ EXAMPLES

➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Sentence Structure
Spanish sentence structure typically follows the Subject+Verb+Object (SVO) pattern, similar to English. However, Spanish is much more flexible, allowing word order changes for emphasis. This includes: dropping subject pronouns and placing adjectives after nouns. (This is just an introduction, this subject is very involved and requires more explanation.)

➜ EXAMPLES

lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 5 # 16

stories.title: Fábulas de Esopo, "El lobo y el cordero"

lines.sentence: Un lobo encontró a un cordero
lines.translation: A wolf found a lamb
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 26 # 1

lines.sentence: que se había extraviado del rebaño
lines.translation: that had strayed from the flock
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 26 # 2

lines.sentence: sintió cierta reticencia sobre quitar la vida
lines.translation: he felt a certain reluctance to take the life
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 26 # 3

lines.translation: of such a defenseless creature
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 26 # 4

lines.translation: without any plausible excuse.
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 27 # 5

lines.translation: So he said to him:
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 27 # 6

lines.sentence: -¿Recuerdas cómo me insultaste el año pasado?
lines.translation: -Do you remember how you insulted me last year?
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 27 # 7

lines.translation: The lamb replied:
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 27 # 8

lines.sentence: -Disculpe, pero eso no es posible porque
lines.translation: -Excuse me, but that's not possible because
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 28 # 9

lines.sentence: el año pasado yo todavía no había nacido.
lines.translation: last year I hadn't been born yet.
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 28 # 10

lines.translation: "Well," objected the wolf,
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 28 # 11

lines.translation: "You feed in my pastures."
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 28 # 12

lines.translation: "That can't be," replied the lamb,
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 28 # 13

lines.sentence: porque nunca he probado la hierba.
lines.translation: “because I've never tried grass.”
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 29 # 14

lines.sentence: -Entonces bebes de mi manantial-continuó el lobo.
lines.translation: "Then you drink from my spring," continued the wolf.
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 29 # 15

lines.translation: "In fact, sir," said the poor lamb,
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 29 # 16

lines.translation: “To this day,
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 29 # 17

lines.sentence: solo he bebido la leche de mi madre.
lines.translation: I have only drank my mother's milk.”
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 29 # 18

lines.translation: "Well, anyway," said the wolf,
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 30 # 19

lines.sentence: no me quedaré sin mi cena.
lines.translation: “I won't go without my dinner.”
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 30 # 20

lines.translation: He pounced on the lamb
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 30 # 21

lines.translation: and devoured him right away.
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 30 # 22

lines.sentence: Las palabras engañosas fácilmente salen a la luz.
lines.translation: Deceptive words easily come to light.
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 30 # 23

stories.title: Fábulas de Esopo, "El lobo con piel de oveja"

lines.sentence: Un lobo decidió disfrazarse para poder
lines.translation: A wolf decided to disguise himself so he could
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 6 # 1

lines.sentence: atacar a un rebaño de ovejas
lines.translation: attack a flock of sheep
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 6 # 2

lines.sentence: sin temor de que lo descubrieran,
lines.translation: without fear of being discovered,
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 6 # 3

lines.sentence: así que se cubrió con la piel
lines.translation: So he covered himself with skin
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 7 # 4

lines.sentence: de una oveja y se mezcló
lines.translation: from a sheep and mingled
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 7 # 5

lines.translation: with the flock while they grazed.
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 7 # 6

lines.translation: He completely deceived the shepherd
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 8 # 7

lines.sentence: y cuando el rebaño fue encerrado
lines.translation: And when the flock was penned up
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 8 # 8

lines.sentence: por la noche, él quedó adentro
lines.translation: That night, he stayed inside
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 8 # 9

lines.translation: with the sheep.
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 9 # 10

lines.translation: That same night the shepherd,
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 9 # 11

lines.sentence: que necesitaba carne para la cena,
lines.translation: who needed meat for dinner,
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 9 # 12

lines.sentence: puso sus manos sobre el lobo y,
lines.translation: laid his hands on the wolf and,
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 10 # 13

lines.translation: believing it was a sheep,
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 10 # 14

lines.sentence: sacó su cuchillo y lo mató en el acto.
lines.translation: pulled out his knife and killed him on the spot.
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 10 # 15

lines.sentence: El que daño busca, daño encuentra.
lines.translation: He who seeks harm, finds harm.
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 10 # 16

lines.translation: Two proud goats met
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 21 # 1

lines.translation: by chance on cliffs opposite
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 21 # 2

lines.translation: of a high mountain range.
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 21 # 3

lines.sentence: Por debajo, entre las rocas del valle,
lines.translation: Below, among the rocks of the valley
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 21 # 4

lines.sentence: pasaba un río turbulento y peligroso.
lines.translation: flowed a turbulent and dangerous river.
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 22 # 5

lines.translation: The only bridge for crossing
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 22 # 6

lines.sentence: el abismo era un árbol caído,
lines.translation: the abyss was a fallen tree,
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 22 # 7

lines.translation: so narrow that two mice
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 22 # 8

lines.sentence: se habrían asustado si hubieran intentado
lines.translation: would have been frightened if they had tried
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 23 # 9

lines.translation: to cross it at the same time.
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 23 # 10

lines.translation: Both goats, stubborn,
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 23 # 11

lines.sentence: se sintieron con el derecho de cruzar primero.
lines.translation: felt the right to cross first.
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 23 # 12

lines.sentence: Así que, poniendo una pezuña a la vez,
lines.translation: So, putting a hoof at a time,
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 24 # 13

lines.sentence: empezaron a caminar sobre el delgado tronco
lines.translation: they began to walk on the thin trunk
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 24 # 14

lines.sentence: hasta que se encontraron frente a frente
lines.translation: until they met face to face
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 24 # 15

lines.translation: in the middle of the bridge.
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 24 # 16

lines.translation: Neither of them wanted to give way,
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 25 # 17

lines.translation: and in the end, both fell
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 25 # 18

lines.sentence: de cabeza a las rugientes aguas.
lines.translation: headfirst into the roaring waters.
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 25 # 19

lines.translation: It is better to give in than to fall
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 25 # 20

lines.translation: into misfortune out of stubbornness.
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 25 # 21

stories.title: Fábulas de Esopo, "La tortuga y el águila"

lines.sentence: Una tortuga, descontenta con su humilde vida
lines.translation: A turtle, unhappy with her humble life
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 16 # 1

lines.translation: and envious of the birds
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 16 # 2

lines.sentence: que veía disfrutar en el aire,
lines.translation: that she saw enjoying themselves in the air,
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 16 # 3

lines.sentence: rogó a un águila que le enseñara a volar.
lines.translation: begged an eagle to teach her to fly.
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 17 # 4

lines.sentence: El águila le dijo que era inútil intentarlo,
lines.translation: The eagle told her it was useless trying,
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 17 # 5

lines.sentence: ya que la naturaleza no le había dado alas;
lines.translation: since nature hadn´t given her wings;
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 17 # 6

lines.translation: but the turtle insisted
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 18 # 7

lines.sentence: con ruegos y promesas de tesoros,
lines.translation: with pleading, and promises of treasures,
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 18 # 8

lines.translation: convinced that it was only
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 18 # 9

lines.sentence: cuestión de aprender el arte de volar.
lines.translation: a matter of learning the art of flying.
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 18 # 10

lines.sentence: Finalmente, el águila accedió a hacer
lines.translation: Finally, the eagle agreed to do it
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 19 # 11

lines.sentence: lo mejor que pudiera y la tomó
lines.translation: as best he could and took her
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 19 # 12

lines.sentence: entre sus garras. Se elevó con ella
lines.translation: between his claws. He rose with her
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 19 # 13

lines.sentence: hasta una gran altura en el cielo,
lines.translation: to a great height in the sky,
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 19 # 14

lines.sentence: la soltó y la desdichada tortuga
lines.translation: he let go of her, and the unfortunate turtle
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 20 # 15

lines.translation: fell headfirst into the sea.
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 20 # 16

lines.translation: If men got everything
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 20 # 17

lines.sentence: lo que desearan, a menudo se arruinarían.
lines.translation: that they wished, they would quickly be ruined.
lines.label: Spanish Story Lines - Set 20 # 18

songsRhymes.title: Diez Deditos, Cuando Vayas al Mercado
songsRhymes.text:
Cuando vayas al mercado,
no compres carne de aquí.
ni de aquí,
ni de aquí,
ni de aquí,
Sólo de aquí.
_(repetir la rima varias veces)_
songsRhymes.translation:
When you go to the marketplace,
don´t buy meat from here
nor here
nor here
nor here
Only from here.
_(repeat the verse several times)_

songsRhymes.title: Diez Deditos, Una Rata Vieja
songsRhymes.text:
Una rata vieja,

que era planchadora,
por planchar su falda

¡se quemó la cola!

Se puso pomada.

Se amarró un trapito.

Y la pobre rata
le quedó un rabito.
songsRhymes.translation:
Pancha, the old rat,

was ironing one day,
and when she pressed her skirt,

she burned her tail away!
She applied some ointment.

She wrapped it in a veil,

but the poor old Pancha,
she lost most of her tail.

songsRhymes.title: Diez Deditos, Mi Gallo
songsRhymes.text:
Mi gallo
se murió
ayer. _(cantar dos veces)_
Ya no cantará
cocorí, cocorá.
Ya no cantará
cocorí, cocorá,
cocorí, corí, cocorí, corá
cocorí, corí, cocorí, corá.
songsRhymes.translation:
My rooster
died
yesterday. _(sing twice)_
He will sing no more
cocorí, cocorá.
He will sing no more
cocorí, cocorá,
cocorí, corí, cocorí, corá
cocorí, corí, cocorí, corá.

songsRhymes.title: Diez Deditos, La Pata
songsRhymes.text:
Este es el baile de la pata.
Haciendo una rueda,
vamos a jugar.

Que pase al centro
una pata.
Todos cantando
cuará, cua, cua.

En la pata izquierda,
bailaba una pata. (_cantar dos veces_)

En la pata derecha,
bailaba una pata. (_cantar dos veces_)

En las dos patas,
bailaba una pata. (_cantar dos veces_)

Y diciendo
cuará, cua, cua,
a otra pata
invitó a bailar. (_cantar dos veces_)
songsRhymes.translation:
This is the dance of the duck.
Making a circle,
we are ready to play.

The first duck
moves to the center.
We all sing together
cuará, cua, cua.

One duck danced, danced, and danced
on the left foot. _(sing twice)_

One duck danced, danced, and danced
on the right foot. _(sing twice)_

One duck danced, danced, and danced
on two feet. _(sing twice)_

And as she sang
cuará, cua, cua.
she invited another duck
to dance. _(sing twice)_

songsRhymes.title: Diez Deditos, Juanito
songsRhymes.text:
Juanito cuando baila,
baila, baila, baila.
Juanito cuando baila,
baila con el dedito,
con el dedito, ito, ito.

Asi baila Juanito.

Juanito cuando baila,
baila, baila, baila.
Juanito cuando baila,
baila con el pie,
con el pie, pie, pie,

con el dedito, ito, ito,

Asi baila Juanito.

Juanito cuando baila...
la rodilla, dilla, dilla...
la cadera, dera, dera...
la mano, mano, mano...
el codo, codo, codo...
el hombro, hombro, hombro...
la cabeza, eza, eza...
songsRhymes.translation:
When little Johnny dances,
he dances, dances, dances,
When little Johnny dances,
he dances with his pinkie,
with his pinkie, pinkie, pinkie.

That´s how little Johnny dances.

When little Johnny dances,
he dances, dances, dances,
When little Johnny dances,
he dances with his foot,
with his foot, foot, foot,

with his pinkie, pinkie, pinkie,

That´s how little Johnny dances.

When little Johnny dances...
knee...
hip...
hand...
elbow...
shoulder...
head...

songsRhymes.title: Diez Deditos, Si Se Puede
songsRhymes.text:
En este mundo
tan lindo y tan grande
yo soy único,
yo soy especial,
lleno de amor
y de inteligencia.

Yo puedo realizar
mis sueños
siendo un buen estudiante
y haciendo siempre mi trabajo
con amor,
con orgullo
y con gusto,
porque sé que
sí se puede!
songsRhymes.translation:
In this beautiful 
and great world
I am unique,
I am very special,
and full of love.
I am intelligent.

I can reach
my goals
by being a good student
and by always doing my work
with love,
with pride,
and with pleasure.
Yes, I can!

lessons.cctBlock:
➜ Cultural Topic - La Feria
Most Spanish speaking countries celebrate regional “ferias” or fairs.  Historically they were a method of exchange and market for agricultural or livestock seasons. They usually include food, music, entertainment, religious and artisanal aspects.  They are bright, colorful and typically run for several days

∞ Video Link: [Feria de Sevilla](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aeHaioZ0vbc), Spain: 8 minutes
∞ Video Link: [Feria de Tonatico](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ARJB0f5K1_0), Mexico: 10 minutes 
Tip: You may need to adjust your settings to display English subtitles.

lessons.cctBlock:
➜ CULTURAL TOPIC - Naranjas
In Spanish culture, small portions of the backyard/land are designated for vegetable and fruit patches; these are known as huertos. They are culturally symbolic and practical in homes.  Such things as providing year-round food or shade in mostly desert-like areas, as found in places like Spain or Mexico. They are a source for gathering and tradition.

∞ Video Link: [Cuidados de Naranja](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BaNRNPUziog) (with a grandmother from Spain). The video is in Spanish but enjoy watching her explain her backyard orange tree. Maybe you will pick up some words.
∞ Video Link: A short video on a [boy picking up an orange](https://youtube.com/shorts/uNtB91ily0Y?si=ZJ7kMt1j6hUWsevU) from his grandfather’s backyard

lessons.grammarInstructions:
➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Nouns & Gender
In Spanish, nouns are either “masculine (el/the)” or “feminine (la/the).” 
Masculine nouns typically end in “o,” while feminine nouns typically end in “a.” (There are exceptions.) 

➜ EXAMPLES

➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Articles (Definite & Indefinite)
Spanish articles (definite and indefinite) must match the noun's gender (masculine/feminine) and number (singular/plural), unlike English. 
Definite articles (el, la, los, las - "the") indicate specific, known items. 
Indefinite articles (un, una, unos, unas - "a, an, some") refer to non-specific or unknown items.

➜ EXAMPLES

➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Plural Nouns
Spanish plural nouns are formed based on the word's final letter, generally by adding -s (for vowels) or -es (for consonants). Special rule for -z: change to -c and add -es. 

➜ EXAMPLES

➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Days of the Week
Days of the week in Spanish (los días de la semana). Unlike in English, the days of the week in Spanish do not begin with capital letters. Days of the week in Spanish are masculine & singular (even though some end in -s.)  lunes (Monday), martes (Tuesday), miércoles (Wednesday), jueves (Thursday), viernes (Friday), sábado (Saturday), domingo (Sunday)

lessons.cctBlock:
➜ CULTURAL TOPIC - Gallinas
Introduction of chickens to Latin American countries provided a good source of protein for families in the form of meat and eggs.  The keeping of chickens continues in many households as a form of maintaining cultural and practical traditions.

∞ Video Link: [Raising chickens in Ecuador](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Dhrv3CUXGc), 3 minutes

lessons.grammarInstructions:
➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Subject Pronouns
Spanish subject pronouns replace nouns to indicate who is performing an action, similar to English ("I," "you," "he/she"). However, unlike English pronouns, they account for gender and levels of formality as well. (This is just an introduction, there is more to learn about Spanish pronouns.)

➜ EXAMPLES

➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Numbers 1-10
Los numeros 1-10. Uno (one), dos (two), tres (three), cuatro (four), cinco (five), seis (six), siete (seven), ocho (eight), nueve (nine) and diez (ten).

➜ EXAMPLES

lessons.grammarInstructions: In Spanish, adjectives must match the noun they describe in both gender (masculine/feminine) and number (singular/plural). Generally, adjectives ending in -o change to -a for feminine, and both add -s or -es to become plural. Adjectives ending in -e or a consonant usually remain the same for gender but change for number.

lessons.grammarInstructions:
➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Adjectives & Agreement
In Spanish, adjectives must match the noun they describe in both gender (masculine/feminine) and number (singular/plural). Generally, adjectives ending in -o change to -a for feminine, and both add -s or -es to become plural. Adjectives ending in -e or a consonant usually remain the same for gender but change for number.

➜ EXAMPLES

➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Sentence Structure
Spanish sentence structure typically follows the Subject+Verb+Object (SVO) pattern, similar to English. However, Spanish is much more flexible, allowing word order changes for emphasis. This includes: dropping subject pronouns and placing adjectives after nouns. (This is just an introduction, this subject is very involved and requires more explanation.)

➜ EXAMPLES

Grammar Concept: Subject Pronouns
Spanish subject pronouns replace nouns to indicate who is performing an action, similar to English ("I," "you," "he/she"). However, unlike English pronouns, they account for gender and levels of formality as well. (This is just an introduction, there is more to learn about Spanish pronouns.)

➜ EXAMPLES

lessons.cctBlock:
➜ CULTURAL TOPIC - Canicas y Trompos
Across Latin America and Spain, they represent a communal, low-cost heritage where kids gather to share stories and trade marbles and play spinning tops.

∞ Video Link: This [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jDF4O_yEQFY) shows a tutorial for a trick with a spinning top “trompos".  Make sure you have the auto translate on for captions.
∞ Video Link: Short [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5V-uOT820vA) of children in Oaxaca playing marbles “canicas”

lessons.grammarInstructions: Spanish question words (interrogativos) are essential for forming questions, they always carry a written accent mark, and are paired with an inverted opening mark (¿). The main question words are qué (what), quién (who), dónde (where), cuándo (when), cómo (how), por qué (why), cuál (which), and cuánto (how much/many).

lessons.cctBlock:
➜ CULTURAL TOPIC - Nopales for Cooking
In Mexican culture, "picando nopales" (dicing cactus pads) represents far more than a culinary step. The prickly pear cactus (nopal) is a profound symbol of resilience and indigenous heritage. It thrives in harsh, arid landscapes and has sustained Mesoamerican communities for thousands of years.

∞ Video Link: This is a [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WJ359L5W988) of a grandma showing how she prepares the nopales she harvests from her home. Remember to have your settings on Spanish to English translation of captions.

lessons.grammarInstructions:
➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Question Words
Spanish question words (interrogativos) are essential for forming questions, they always carry a written accent mark, and are paired with an inverted opening mark (¿). The main question words are qué (what), quién (who), dónde (where), cuándo (when), cómo (how), por qué (why), cuál (which), and cuánto (how much/many).

➜ EXAMPLES

➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Negative Sentence Structure
Spanish negative sentences are formed by placing "no" directly before the conjugated verb. Unlike English, Spanish requires a negative word before the verb.

➜ EXAMPLES

➜ GRAMMAR
Grammar Concept: Months Part 1
The months of the year (los meses del año) in Spanish are masculine, and unlike in English they are not capitalized unless they start a sentence.  They are: enero(January), febrero (February), marzo (March), abril (April), mayo (May), junio (June), julio (July), agosto (August), septiembre (September), octubre (October), noviembre (November) and diciembre (December).

terms.content:
· Picture Study
• Tell all you can about the picture La Feria de Reynoso using Spanish. (Students should be able to provide at least 3 distinct phrases in Spanish describing the picture).

· Literature 
• Choose one of the following sentences to read out loud, sketch or perform gestures for:
Sentence 1: "así que se cubrió con la piel" 
(So he covered himself with his skin) 
OR
Sentence 2: "Saltó una y otra vez, pero fue".
(He jumped again and again, but it was)

· Songs, Rhymes 
• Choose a song/rhyme to sing/recite for your teacher.
Song/Rhyme Choices: Juanito OR Si Se Puede

·  Picture Study
• Choose a picture from the options below and tell all you can about the picture using
Spanish vocabulary. (Students should be able to provide at least 3 distinct phrases in Spanish describing
the picture).
Picture Choices: La Cena or Cumpleaños

· Literature
• Choose one of the following sentences to read aloud, sketch, or perform gestures for.
Sentence 1: Rebuznó ruidosamente en triunfo.
